position_in_era.historical_role: Immediate heir to the Black Sabbath self-titled template: the opening guitar-bass unison riff at half-tempo, followed by a sudden speed-up, is the first documented use of tempo as dramatic architecture in heavy metal. Demonstrates that the weight-first aesthetic can encompass multiple tempos without losing its gravitational centre.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded June 1970 at Regent Sound Studios and Island Studios, London, produced by Rodger Bain. The song was originally titled 'Walpurgis' — Vertigo requested a title change. Iommi's opening riff is in the same C# tuning as the self-titled track. The song is 7:54 — Sabbath's first long-form riff composition.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Iommi drives the arrangement; Butler's anti-war lyric (Generals gathered in their masses / just like witches at black masses) sets the political dimension that Sabbath songs would carry from this point. Ward's drumming is notably more dynamic here than on the self-titled — the tempo shift in the middle section is his contribution.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Iommi: Gibson SG (C# tuning); Butler: Fender Precision Bass; Ward: Ludwig drums; Osbourne: lead vocal. The riff structure alternates between a slow E-form power chord descent and a faster mid-section in a different key — two riff-worlds cohabiting one song.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Released as the opening track of the Paranoid album (September 1970). Originally planned as the album's title track. The song's anti-Vietnam War politics made it a campus anthem in the US despite minimal radio play. Widely cited alongside the self-titled as the two founding documents of doom metal.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: The Paranoid album was recorded in two days. 'War Pigs' and the self-titled 'Black Sabbath' together account for the two gravitational poles of heavy metal: supernatural dread (self-titled) and political fury (War Pigs).
